pg139_n0019: This section presents the meaning, purposes, and common users of financial statements.
pg139_n0021: The meaning and purpose of financial statements
pg139_n0025: Financial statements are statements that are prepared periodically to present the results of the business for the period.
pg139_n0027: While there are five components of financial statements, but the focus is on two, namely income statement and a statement of financial position.
pg139_n0028: The income statement, which is also known as a statement of profit or loss, is prepared in order to determine a profit or a loss made by the business in a particular accounting period.
pg139_n0029: On the other hand, the statement of financial position which is also known as a balance sheet, is prepared in order to show the financial position of a business by considering the balances of assets, liabilities and capital.
pg139_n0031: Some businesses, for example, companies, are required by law to prepare financial statements.
pg140_n0003: statements may not be legally required (except for tax purposes), but the needs of the owners would be met through the use of financial statements, especially in evaluating performance of the business for the period.
pg140_n0004: There are also other users who would benefit from the financial statements of a business.
pg140_n0005: This is because their understanding of financial and operational affairs of the business can be useful in making informed decisions.
pg140_n0009: Detailed descriptions of the purpose of preparing financial statements are to:
pg140_n0013: Many businesses are established for the purpose of making profits.
pg140_n0014: Therefore, it is important to measure whether this objective has been achieved.
pg140_n0015: This is because, owners will have an opportunity to evaluate whether the management has met their targets or not.
pg140_n0016: It will also assist owners in making decision on whether to continue with the business or not.
pg140_n0018: Show the financial position of the business
pg140_n0020: When a business gets into a difficult financial position, for example, being overburdened by liabilities, it may face the risk of closure due to inability to pay debts.
pg140_n0021: Similarly, when the business has a large proportion of its assets on non-productive assets, this creates a possibility of failure of the business in the future.
pg140_n0022: On the other hand, a good proportion of productive assets forecasts a bright future for the business.
pg140_n0026: These are assets existing in the business but not fully utilised to generate revenue.
pg140_n0027: For example, a large office building in excess of the business requirements may represent a non-productive asset.
pg140_n0029: Help in assessing the efficiency of business operations
pg140_n0031: Efficiency of business operations is useful in ensuring that the business achieves its profit-making objective.
pg140_n0032: Examples of efficiency measures include assets utilisation and frequency of stock movements, stock turnover.
pg140_n0033: Assets utilisation is usually used in measuring how well the business is using its available assets to make money.
pg140_n0034: Stock turnover is a measure used for establishing how many times a business has sold and replaced its inventory during a given period.
pg140_n0035: Figures used to calculate ratios for these measures are usually obtained from financial statements.
pg140_n0036: When there is an unsatisfactory level of efficiency, the business can plan ways to improve its performance.
pg140_n0040: Amounts of different taxes payable by the business are computed from the figures obtained from financial statements.
pg140_n0041: Profit and sales figures provide a reasonable basis for calculating taxes related to turnover or profits.
pg140_n0042: These figures can be easily obtained from the business financial statements.
pg141_n0005: Planning and evaluation are among the main functions of management.
pg141_n0006: Financial statements are useful in evaluating the performance of a business for the period.
pg141_n0007: This can be done through comparing the targets established at the beginning of the year with the actual results that are obtained from the financial statements.
pg141_n0008: Moreover, the performance of the current year can form the basis for setting plans for the next year.
pg141_n0010: Establish the riskiness of the business
pg141_n0012: Different stakeholders dealing with the business, for example, banks, customers, and suppliers will need to be sure about the risk associated with the business.
pg141_n0013: In this context, a risk may be defined as the probability that actual results will differ from the expected results.
pg141_n0014: Traditionally, risk has been defined in terms of the possibility of danger, loss, injury or other negative outcomes.
pg141_n0015: For example, customers would want to be assured of steady supplies of goods, while banks and suppliers would want to be sure of the ability of the business to settle their debts.
pg141_n0016: Since financial statements provide the results of business performance, they are usually considered as a reliable source of information.
pg141_n0017: The information will help stakeholders to have answers for their questions including the risks associated with the business.
pg141_n0021: Financial statements are used by various stakeholders, including investors, creditors, management, and regulators, to assess the enterprise's financial health and make informed decisions.
pg141_n0022: The three common components of financial statements are:
pg141_n0024: Income statement, profit or loss statement
pg141_n0026: The income statement presents the financial performance of a business resulting from its operating activities over a specific period, for example, a quarter or a year.
pg141_n0027: It provides a summary of revenues, expenses, and the resulting profit or loss.
pg141_n0028: The income statement follows the basic formula:
pg141_n0031: Key figures included in the income statement are:
pg141_n0038: Cost of goods sold, C O G S, applicable for businesses selling products,
pg141_n0041: Gross profit, revenues minus cost of goods sold,
pg141_n0044: Operating expenses, selling, general, and administrative expenses,
pg141_n0047: Operating income, gross profit minus operating expenses,
pg141_n0050: Other income and expenses, interest income, interest expenses, and
pg141_n0053: Profit or loss for the period.
pg141_n0055: Statement of financial position, balance sheet
pg141_n0057: The statement of financial position presents the financial position of a business at a specific point in time, usually the end of a quarter or a year.
pg141_n0058: It shows what the resources of the business, assets, what it owes to
pg142_n0003: other, liabilities, and the residual interest of the owners, equity.
pg142_n0005: The statement of financial position follows the accounting equation:
pg142_n0007: Key elements of a statement of financial position include:
pg142_n0011: Assets, current assets and non-current assets
pg142_n0014: Liabilities, current liabilities and non-current liabilities
pg142_n0017: Capital or Equity, fund invested in a business for example, initial capital and retained earnings
pg142_n0021: The cash flow statement provides an overview of an enterprise's cash inflows and outflows over a specific period.
pg142_n0022: It shows how cash is generated and used by operating, investing, and financing activities of the enterprise during the period.
pg142_n0023: The cash flow statement is divided into three sections:
pg142_n0027: Operating activities: Cash flows resulting from day-to-day business operations, including cash received from customers and cash paid to suppliers and employees.
pg142_n0030: Investing activities: Cash flows resulting from buying or selling long-term assets, such as property, equipment or investments.
pg142_n0033: Financing activities: Cash flows resulting from transactions with the enterprise's owners and loan providers, including issuance or repurchase of shares, acquisition or repayment of loan as well as payment of dividends.
pg142_n0035: These financial statements components are critical for assessing an enterprise’s financial performance, liquidity, solvency, and overall financial health.
pg142_n0036: Together, they provide a comprehensive view of the enterprise’s financial position and serve as valuable tools for decision-making and financial analysis.
pg142_n0037: In this chapter, only income statement and statement of financial positions will be discussed, while cashflow statements will be discussed in higher forms.
pg142_n0041: An income statement is a statement prepared at the end of an accounting period to calculate the profit or loss made.
pg142_n0042: The statement calculates profit or loss for the period by comparing revenue earned during the period and expenses incurred during the same period.
pg142_n0043: It is therefore in the income statement where the matching principle, as highlighted in chapter one is applied.
pg142_n0047: The purpose of preparing an income statement is to calculate the amount of profit or loss for a particular period.
pg142_n0048: Profit or loss for a merchandising business is calculated in two stages.
pg142_n0049: The first stage compares the amount of net sales and cost of goods sold to obtain the gross profit or loss.
pg142_n0050: The second stage compares the gross profit, obtained from the first stage, and other incomes with different expenses incurred in operating the business during the period.
pg142_n0051: The result is the profit or loss for the period.
pg143_n0003: Terms used in an income statement
pg143_n0005: Terms used in an income statement are explained as follows:
pg143_n0009: The figure of net sales is made by two aspects which are sales and sales returns.
pg143_n0010: The sales figure is the credit balance transferred from the sales account in the general ledger.
pg143_n0011: It is the total of all sales, both credit and cash, made during the period under consideration.
pg143_n0012: Sales returns are those goods that were previously sold to a customer but were later returned due to different reasons.
pg143_n0013: Therefore, the net sales is calculated by taking sales less the sales returns, which is also known as returns inwards.
pg143_n0017: The figure for net purchases is obtained after taking into consideration several aspects.
pg143_n0018: The first aspect is the debit balance found in the account of purchases itself.
pg143_n0019: This figure is the total purchases, cash and credit, done in the whole accounting period.
pg143_n0021: The second component included in the calculation of the net purchases figure is the purchases returns or returns outwards.
pg143_n0022: Purchases returns refer to those goods which were previously purchased by the entity but were later returned to the supplier due to several reasons.
pg143_n0023: It should be noted that the figure for purchases shows the total amount, credit and cash, of purchases made without deducting those goods that were returned to the supplier.
pg143_n0024: Therefore, to determine at a net purchases figure, purchases returns must be deducted from the purchases figure.
pg143_n0026: The complete equation of net purchases is stated as net purchases is equal to purchases less purchases returns.
pg143_n0028: Because of the objective of the process, that is, calculation of the cost of goods sold, another item considered as part of such cost is the carriage inwards costs.
pg143_n0029: These are costs of transferring or transporting the purchased goods from where they were procured to the premises of the enterprise.
pg143_n0030: In simple terms, the cost of goods purchased is the total of the cost paid to purchase such goods plus the transportation cost of bringing those goods to the enterprise's premises.
pg143_n0031: For example, the supplier sold goods for T Z S one hundred thousand and T Z S ten thousand is incurred by the buyer to transport such goods from the supplier’s premises to his or her premises.
pg143_n0032: In this case, the cost of such goods is not only T Z S one hundred thousand but is T Z S one hundred and ten thousand, T Z S one hundred thousand plus ten thousand.
pg143_n0036: An opening inventory is the inventory of goods held by the entity at the beginning of the accounting period.
pg143_n0037: On the other hand, a closing inventory is the inventory of goods held by the entity at the end of the accounting period.
pg143_n0038: For instance, suppose the accounting period of the enterprise starts on first January and ends on thirty-first December.
pg143_n0039: The opening inventory of such an enterprise would be considered as the inventory held by that enterprise on first January, while the closing inventory would be considered as the inventory held by that enterprise on thirty-first December.
pg144_n0003: inventory held by that enterprise on thirty-first December would be the opening inventory of the enterprise in the following year.
pg144_n0005: Cost of goods available for sale
pg144_n0007: The figure of the cost of goods available for sale is the sum of the figure of opening inventory and the figure of net purchases.
pg144_n0011: The figure of the cost of goods sold is the difference between the figure of the cost of goods available for sale and closing inventory.
pg144_n0012: In other words, the cost of goods sold is obtained by deducting the cost of closing inventory from the cost of goods available for sale.
pg144_n0016: The figure of gross profit is obtained by deducting the cost of goods sold from the net sales figure.
pg144_n0017: Gross profit is the profit obtained by the enterprises from trading activities only without including other operation expenses.
pg144_n0021: The figure of gross loss is obtained by deducting net sales from the cost of goods sold.
pg144_n0022: Gross loss is the excess of cost of goods sold over net sales.
pg144_n0024: Profit or loss for the period
pg144_n0026: Profit or loss can be computed by taking the total revenue minus the total expenses for the period.
pg144_n0027: The excess of total revenue over total expenses is usually termed as a profit.
pg144_n0028: Alternatively, the excess of total expenses over total revenue is termed as a loss.
pg144_n0032: A gross profit is the difference between the net sales and the cost of goods sold.
pg144_n0033: The figure of the net sales is the balance of the sales account in the general ledger at the end of a period.
pg144_n0034: However, it may happen that some of the goods sold during the period were returned.
pg144_n0035: The figure to be used in the income statement in this case will be that of the net sales, that is, sales less the sales returns.
pg144_n0036: The sales returns figure is obtained from the sales returns account in the general ledger.
pg144_n0038: As for the figure of the cost of goods sold, the main ingredient is the value of the purchases.
pg144_n0039: In some cases, the figure of net purchases will be used instead.
pg144_n0040: For the same reasons as discussed in the case of sales returns, if there are some goods which were returned to suppliers, there will be a need to deduct them from the purchases figure.
pg144_n0041: In addition to the figure of purchases, net purchases, this figure can be adjusted with the cost incurred by the business to transport the goods to its premises.
pg144_n0042: This cost is also known as carriage inwards.
pg144_n0043: The figure of this cost is the balance of the carriage inwards account found in the general ledger.

pg144_n0048: This would also mean that gross profit equals net sales less net purchases.

pg150_n0012: Unlike the income statement that reports a financial performance (profit or loss) for a period, a statement of financial position shows the financial position of an enterprise at a specific date.
pg150_n0013: The specific date is the end of the accounting period.
pg150_n0014: The statement of a financial position is therefore prepared by enterprises to present its financial position as at the date indicated on that statement.
pg150_n0016: The statement of financial position of the enterprise shows the relationship between assets, liabilities and capital.
pg150_n0017: You will recall that, the basic accounting equation states that assets are equal to liabilities plus capital.
pg150_n0018: The statement of financial position, therefore, aims at showing how this equation stands at the end of the accounting period, considering in each of these elements.
pg150_n0019: The statement of financial position is referred to as such because it shows the assets of the enterprise and how such assets have been financed that is proportions of liabilities and capital.
pg150_n0021: Preparing a statement of financial position
pg150_n0023: When preparing a statement of financial position, the value of each category of assets and liabilities is usually taken from the general ledger balances.
pg150_n0024: To make it easy for the users to understand well the financial position of the business, there is an orderly system used in presenting assets and liabilities, rather than listing them randomly.
pg150_n0025: The common methods used in presenting assets and liabilities are explained in the following sections.
pg150_n0027: Approaches of presenting assets and liabilities
pg150_n0029: There are two approaches that are commonly used to present assets and liabilities in the statement of financial position.
pg150_n0030: The methods are such that the assets and liabilities are listed according to the length of time taken to pay the debts (in case of liabilities) or, in case of an asset, the length of time it will take

pg151_n0003: for it to be turned into cash.
pg151_n0004: The length of time it takes for an asset to be turned into cash is an indicator of liquidity.
pg151_n0005: Cash is considered to be the most liquid asset.
pg151_n0006: This means that assets that take a shorter time to be converted into cash are considered to be more liquid than those that take a longer time.
pg151_n0009: It is a measure of the ability of a business to meet its financial obligations as they fall due.
pg151_n0010: One of the indicators of liquidity is time spent to convert its assets into cash.
pg151_n0012: The first approach commonly used to presenting the assets and liabilities is to list the assets and liabilities in order of liquidity.
pg151_n0013: The second method involves the grouping of assets and liabilities by considering whether they are current or non-current items.
pg151_n0015: Listing in the order of liquidity
pg151_n0017: This approach is mostly used by financial institutions such as banks.
pg151_n0018: Using this approach, the business lists its assets starting from the most liquid assets or liabilities to the least liquid ones.
pg151_n0019: Alternatively, the assets and liabilities can be listed starting with the least liquid to the most liquid ones.
pg151_n0020: Under this approach, liabilities will be listed starting with those that take the shortest time to be settled to the ones that take the longest time to be settled, and vice versa.

pg152_n0003: Grouping assets and liabilities into current and non-current classification
pg152_n0005: Grouping assets and liabilities into current and non-current classification is usually done with reference to the accounting period under consideration.
pg152_n0006: Under this classification, the following groups of assets and liabilities will be considered.
pg152_n0010: Current assets include cash and other assets that are held primarily for the purpose of trading.
pg152_n0011: Usually, it is expected that they will be realised in the entity’s normal operating cycle, and within the next accounting period.
pg152_n0012: In other words, current assets are either cash, at bank or in hand, or others that would be converted into cash within the next accounting period under the normal operations of the business.
pg152_n0013: Examples of current assets include inventory, accounts receivable, cash at bank and cash in hand.
pg152_n0017: Non-current assets are all assets other than current assets, which are expected to be used in supporting business operations for more than one year or accounting period.
pg152_n0018: Examples of non-current assets include land, building, furniture, vehicles, plants and machinery owned by the business.
pg152_n0022: Current liabilities are those liabilities that need to be paid within one year or accounting period.
pg152_n0023: For this reason, current liabilities are also known as short term debts.
pg152_n0024: Examples of current liabilities include creditors or trade payables and bank overdrafts.
pg152_n0028: Non-current liabilities are all liabilities other than current liabilities that become due, they are supposed to be paid, beyond one year.
pg152_n0029: For this reason, non-current liabilities are also known as long term debts.
pg152_n0030: Examples of non-current liabilities include bank loans and a term loan from a friend.

pg158_n0015: The information presented in the financial statements is useful to different users of financial statements depending on what the information is needed for.
pg158_n0016: The following is a list of common users of financial statements and the reasons for seeking such information.
pg158_n0019: Managers are supervisors of enterprises on daily basis.
pg158_n0020: They are interested in the information presented in the financial statements to know the performance of the business.
pg158_n0021: The financial statements may also be useful for managers in making future plans.
pg158_n0024: These are the people who invested their money or other resources into the business with the objectives of making a profit.
pg158_n0025: Therefore, they will be interested in the information presented on the financial statements because it enables them to evaluate their business with reference to the targeted profit.
pg158_n0026: Prospective investors or buyers of the business
pg158_n0028: These are people who are interested in committing their money to invest or purchase part or the whole business in order to benefit from the profit generated.
pg158_n0029: Before the prospective investor or buyer purchases a business, he or she would want to see its financial statements to evaluate its ability to make profits.
pg158_n0030: This information is very important in making informed decision on whether to invest in the business or not.
pg158_n0033: A person (or entity) who puts his or her money into business in order to become one of the owners for the purpose of getting a share of the profit generated.
pg158_n0036: Tax officers from tax authorities, such as the Tanzania Revenue Authority, T R A, and the Zanzibar Revenue Authority, Z R A, would want to see the financial statements of an enterprise to establish appropriateness of calculations and the amount of tax to be paid by the enterprise.
pg158_n0039: Different banks that the entrepreneur may approach for loans and other services would want to know the performance trend of the business in order to make
pg159_n0003: decisions on whether to lend or not.
pg159_n0004: The bank would, for example, want to see the financial statements to assess whether the business can repay the loan that it is applying for.
pg159_n0008: Creditors or payables are suppliers of goods or services, who sell goods or provide services to the business on credit.
pg159_n0009: Creditors are interested in the information presented in the financial statements because they want to assess the ability of debtors to pay for the goods and services supplied on credit when due.
pg159_n0013: Debtors or receivables are enterprises or individuals who purchase goods or services from the business on credit.
pg159_n0014: Debtors do not usually use the financial statements of their creditors, but sometimes they need them, especially cash flow statements, to check the capability of these creditors to regularly supply goods, especially when dealing with tender businesses.
pg159_n0018: Basic financial statements are key documents that provide a comprehensive overview of a business financial performance and position.
pg159_n0019: These statements are crucial for stakeholders, including investors, creditors, and managers, to assess the business financial health and make informed decisions.
pg159_n0020: Financial statements include, among others, statement of financial position, balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement.
pg159_n0022: The statement of financial position presents a summary of the enterprise's financial position at a specific point in time, detailing its assets, liabilities, and equity.
pg159_n0023: It demonstrates the accounting equation, assets equals liabilities plus equity, and shows how the business’ resources are financed.
pg159_n0024: The income statement, on the other hand, presents the businesses revenues, expenses, and net income, or net loss, over a specific period, typically a quarter or a year.
pg159_n0025: It reveals the businesses profitability by comparing revenue with expenses.
pg159_n0026: The cash flow statement illustrates the business cash inflows and outflows during a given period.
pg159_n0027: It categorising them into operating, investing, and financing activities.
pg159_n0028: This statement shows the business ability to generate and manage cash, which is vital for its sustainability and growth.
pg159_n0029: Together, these basic financial statements provide a clear and comprehensive picture of a business’ financial performance and position, allowing stakeholders to gauge its profitability, solvency, and liquidity.

pg009_n0007_easy_read: Book-keeping gives students important skills and knowledge for their future careers.
pg009_n0008_easy_read:
When students learn Book-keeping principles and concepts well, they build a strong base.
This helps them understand financial transactions and record them correctly.
pg009_n0009_easy_read:
When students understand Book-keeping well, they can help a business succeed financially.
They can also manage their own money matters better.
pg009_n0010_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn the concept of Book-keeping.
You will focus on:
- the origin of Book-keeping
- the meaning of Book-keeping
- the scope of Book-keeping
- the purpose of Book-keeping
- the types of Book-keeping methods or systems
- the relationship between Book-keeping and other disciplines
- the basic terms used in Book-keeping
pg009_n0011_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you understand why it is important to keep records of business financial transactions.
They will also help you negotiate and think clearly during business deals.
pg009_n0016_easy_read: Think about how your parents or guardians keep records of their income and expenses.
pg009_n0019_easy_read: Business is one of the common occupations that is important for day-to-day income in any country.
pg009_n0020_easy_read:
Many businesses are run by large companies, both locally and internationally.
But many people in business also run small businesses.
pg009_n0021_easy_read: We deal with small businesses every day when we buy the things we need each day.
pg009_n0022_easy_read:
Typical small businesses include:
- hawkers
- vegetable vendors
- street retail shops
- shoe shining
- newspaper vending
- salon businesses, open bracket hair dressers, close bracket
- artisans
- many others
pg009_n0023_easy_read:
All these businesses carry out different financial transactions.
They:
- buy inputs or materials
- do some processing
- sell goods or provide services
pg009_n0025_easy_read: Book-keeping is necessary for every business enterprise.
pg009_n0026_easy_read:
Business operators or owners may not have proper knowledge of Book-keeping.
Even so, they may still use Book-keeping principles without knowing it to achieve different objectives of their business.
pg010_n0004_easy_read: Take the example of Missus Chaza, who starts a food vending business called Swahili-bites.
pg010_n0005_easy_read: This business works near Jenga-afya Secondary School in Maruku.
pg010_n0006_easy_read: The business will need equipment such as cookers, pans, and serving utensils.
pg010_n0007_easy_read: The business will also need furniture such as benches, tables, and cupboards.
pg010_n0008_easy_read: The business will buy raw food and cook it for sale.
pg010_n0009_easy_read: To help the food business run well, Missus Chaza may need to do the following:
pg010_n0012_easy_read: Hire some cooks and service attendants.
pg010_n0020_easy_read: Record credit sales if some food is sold on credit.
pg010_n0022_easy_read: All these activities will involve money moving in or out.
pg010_n0023_easy_read: Later, Mrs Chaza will need to check if the business is meeting its objectives.
pg010_n0024_easy_read: One likely objective is to make a profit from the business.
pg010_n0025_easy_read: This means that Mrs Chaza will need to calculate whether her business has made a profit or not.
pg010_n0026_easy_read: To find out the profit or loss, Mrs Chaza must compare the sales revenue from selling food with the cost of the materials and services used.
pg010_n0027_easy_read:
To do this, Mrs Chaza needs to keep records of:
- money paid for each material and service
- money received from selling food to customers
pg010_n0028_easy_read:
In simple words, Book-keeping means keeping records of:
- money spent on each material and service
- money received from selling goods to customers
pg010_n0032_easy_read: Book-keeping started in ancient civilisations such as Sumeria and Egypt.
pg010_n0033_easy_read: These societies developed systems to record and track transactions and goods exchanged.
pg010_n0034_easy_read: Over time, Book-keeping principles grew into different techniques through the work of Greek and Roman entrepreneurs.
pg010_n0035_easy_read: In the medieval period, Luca Pacioli played an important role in fourteen ninety-four in promoting the double entry Book-keeping system.
pg010_n0036_easy_read: This introduction was an important development that changed the field of Book-keeping.
pg010_n0037_easy_read: Since then, Book-keeping has continued to change and adapt to changing economic systems and new technology.
pg010_n0038_easy_read:
Today, Book-keeping is still a vital part of accounting and financial management. It helps to:
- keep records
- support financial reporting
- support analysis
- maintain transparency and accountability in financial matters
pg010_n0042_easy_read: Book-keeping is an important part of the accounting process.
pg010_n0043_easy_read: It plays an important role in the early stages of the accounting process.
pg010_n0044_easy_read: As explained earlier, Book-keeping is the recording of business financial transactions in books of accounts in an orderly way.
pg010_n0045_easy_read: In principle, every transaction must be recorded in a systematic way.
pg011_n0004_easy_read: This recording includes correct classification based on the type of transaction.
pg011_n0005_easy_read: The final result of Book-keeping is net figures or balances in the ledger accounts.
pg011_n0006_easy_read: This helps to show whether the business made a profit or a loss and what the financial position of the business is.
pg011_n0007_easy_read: Book-keeping also helps to manage credit dealings, control the business properly, and calculate taxes correctly.
pg011_n0008_easy_read: So, Book-keeping is the systematic recording, organising, and tracking of financial transactions and activities in a business.
pg011_n0012_easy_read:
Visit nearby food vendors or mobile money service shops.
Look at the different activities that involve keeping financial records.
pg011_n0013_easy_read: After that, read textbooks or reliable online sources.
pg011_n0014_easy_read:
Compare what you have seen with what you have read.
Then write your understanding of Book-keeping in your own words.
pg011_n0018_easy_read:
The Book-keeping process covers:
- recording financial transactions
- classifying financial transactions
- organising financial records
- keeping financial records up to date
pg011_n0019_easy_read:
Book-keeping plays a central role in giving accurate financial information for:
- decision making
- legal and regulatory compliance
- financial analysis within a business
pg011_n0023_easy_read: The purpose of Book-keeping is to help a business record and track the financial transactions of an enterprise or business activities.
pg011_n0024_easy_read:
Book-keeping gives clear and organised records of business financial transactions, including:
- sales
- purchases
- consumption
- payments
- receipts
pg011_n0025_easy_read: The specific purposes of Book-keeping include:
pg011_n0029_easy_read: Financial records: Book-keeping makes sure all financial records are properly documented and easy to get when needed.
pg011_n0030_easy_read:
Book-keeping gives a full record of financial transactions.
This helps to keep a clear and accurate account of the enterprise’s financial activities.
pg011_n0033_easy_read: Compliance and legal requirements: Book-keeping plays an important role in meeting legal and regulatory duties.
pg011_n0034_easy_read:
Organised and proper financial records are necessary for:
- preparing tax returns
- meeting financial reporting requirements
pg011_n0037_easy_read: Financial management: Book-keeping provides information for effective financial management.
pg011_n0038_easy_read:
It helps businesses to:
- track expenses
- monitor cash flow
- evaluate financial resources
pg011_n0039_easy_read:
When an enterprise has up-to-date financial records, it can make informed decisions about:
- investment
- budgeting
- resource allocation
pg011_n0042_easy_read:
Facilitating business decision making: Book-keeping gives information about:
- revenue generation
- cost management
- profitability
pg011_n0043_easy_read: This information helps in making sound business decisions.
pg012_n0005_easy_read:
Management can use accurate financial data to:
- analyse different parts of the business
- find areas that need improvement
- make good decisions to help the business grow
pg012_n0009_easy_read: Book-keeping is important to business owners and to other people outside the business in these ways:
pg012_n0013_easy_read: Book-keeping helps a business know if it is making a profit or a loss.
pg012_n0014_easy_read:
This is possible because Book-keeping helps the business keep financial records that are:
- complete
- accurate
- up to date
These records are used to prepare financial statements.
pg012_n0015_easy_read:
Look at the example of Mrs Chaza on page two.
Book-keeping helps the business calculate the profit or loss made from the food vending business for any period.
pg012_n0019_easy_read: Many businesses work on both a cash basis and a credit basis.
pg012_n0020_easy_read:
For example, Mrs Chaza would sell most of her food for cash.
But sometimes she would sell food to some customers on credit.
pg012_n0021_easy_read: In the same way, Mrs Chaza may buy some raw food on credit from the market.
pg012_n0022_easy_read: In practice, many businesses have many transactions on credit.
pg012_n0023_easy_read:
Book-keeping helps businesses keep proper records of credit transactions.
It also helps the business know:
- how much each debtor owes the business
- how much the business owes each creditor
pg012_n0024_easy_read: A business can keep these records in a systematic way by following Book-keeping principles.
pg012_n0027_easy_read: Debtor: A debtor is a customer who bought goods from a business on credit and promises to pay later.
pg012_n0029_easy_read: Creditor: A creditor is a supplier who sold goods or provided a service to the business on credit, to be paid later.
pg012_n0033_easy_read: For a business owner to control the business well, the owner needs to keep proper financial records.
pg012_n0034_easy_read: In the long run, these records help the owner decide whether to expand or reduce the business.
pg012_n0035_easy_read:
If Mrs Chaza sells:
- breakfast
- lunch
- dinner
proper record keeping can help her decide how much effort to give to each menu.
pg012_n0036_easy_read: Also, if food is sold in more than one location or centre, Book-keeping can show from the sales records whether sales at one centre or another centre should be expanded or reduced.
pg012_n0037_easy_read: Book-keeping can also help the owner see if money, foodstuff, or materials may have been stolen or misused.
pg012_n0038_easy_read: This can help the owner decide what corrective measures to take where necessary.
pg013_n0005_easy_read: Book-keeping helps the owner know the financial position of the business.
pg013_n0006_easy_read:
It helps the owner understand:
- the value of assets
- the value of liabilities
- the amount of capital the owner contributed
pg013_n0007_easy_read: This can help show whether the business has grown or not.
pg013_n0008_easy_read: Knowing the financial position of a business can also help when applying for a loan or other credit to expand the business.
pg013_n0012_easy_read: Tax authorities such as the Tanzania Revenue Authority, T R A, and Zanzibar Revenue Authority, Z R A, need to receive and check the books of accounts of every enterprise that operates in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg013_n0013_easy_read: This is important for calculating the amount of tax the enterprises should pay.
pg013_n0014_easy_read: Tax laws in Tanzania use a self-assessment system. This means that, for some taxes, the taxpayer must calculate the tax payable.
pg013_n0015_easy_read: So, keeping financial records properly helps both the owner and the tax authorities assess the amount of tax payable.
pg013_n0016_easy_read: Tax laws in Tanzania also punish businesses that do not keep financial documents and records properly.
pg013_n0017_easy_read: So, book-keeping can help the business save money that it would otherwise pay as penalties for not keeping financial records.

pg013_n0027_easy_read: A business finds out its profit or loss, and meets other objectives, by preparing financial statements.
pg013_n0028_easy_read: The whole process that businesses use to prepare financial statements from accounting records is called the accounting cycle.
pg013_n0029_easy_read: The accounting cycle has eight stages. Book-keeping plays an active role in the first seven stages.
pg013_n0030_easy_read: The stages in the accounting cycle are summarised below:
pg013_n0034_easy_read: Identifying transactions by using the source documents,
pg014_n0004_easy_read: two. Record the transactions in the books of prime entry.
pg014_n0006_easy_read: three. Post transactions to the ledger accounts.
pg014_n0010_easy_read: five. Make adjusting entries and correct errors.
pg014_n0012_easy_read: six. Extract the adjusted trial balance.
pg014_n0016_easy_read: eight. Analyse and interpret the financial statements.
pg014_n0020_easy_read:
This is the first stage in the accounting process.
At this stage, financial transactions are identified and supported by source documents such as:
- receipts
- payment vouchers
- invoices
- cheques
- debit note
- credit note
pg014_n0021_easy_read:
For a transaction to be identified and supported, it must:
- have a financial value
- affect at least two items in the accounting equation
pg014_n0025_easy_read:
The second stage is to record these transactions in the books of prime entry.
These books are also called books of original entry.
pg014_n0026_easy_read:
The transaction is first recorded in these books.
After that, it is recorded or posted somewhere else.
pg014_n0027_easy_read:
This book will focus on six types of books of prime entry:
- sales journal
- purchases journal
- sales returns journal
- purchase returns journal
- general journal
- cash book
pg014_n0031_easy_read: The third stage in the accounting cycle is posting transactions to the ledger accounts.
pg014_n0032_easy_read: In this process, entries first recorded in the books of prime entry are posted to the ledger accounts.
pg014_n0033_easy_read: Entries are posted to the correct ledger accounts by following the double entry system of Book-keeping.
pg014_n0037_easy_read: The fourth stage in the accounting cycle is extracting the trial balance.
pg014_n0038_easy_read: The trial balance is a list prepared on a specific date. It shows the net figures or balances of all general ledger accounts.
pg014_n0039_easy_read: The account balances taken from the general ledger are listed in the debit and credit columns of the trial balance.
pg014_n0040_easy_read: The debit and credit columns must be equal.
pg014_n0041_easy_read: The trial balance is usually prepared to check the arithmetic accuracy of double entries made in the ledger accounts. It also gives a full list of balances for preparing financial statements.
pg014_n0045_easy_read: An account is a summary record of business transactions.
pg014_n0046_easy_read: An account can be shown on a page of a ledger book.
pg014_n0049_easy_read: Debit and Credit are two terms used to describe the two sides of an account: - the left-hand side, which is Debit - the right-hand side, which is Credit
pg015_n0003_easy_read: Double entry is a system of book-keeping. In this system, each business transaction is recorded in the books of accounts.
pg015_n0007_easy_read: A trial balance should show some errors made when people first record transactions in the books of prime entry or when they do double entry in the ledger.
pg015_n0009_easy_read: This process goes together with making any needed changes to the balances before preparing the financial statements.
pg015_n0013_easy_read: After correcting the errors and making adjusting entries, you need to prepare the adjusted trial balance.
pg015_n0014_easy_read: The adjusted trial balance has the balances used to prepare the financial statements.
pg015_n0018_easy_read: Financial statements are prepared using figures taken from the adjusted trial balance.
pg015_n0019_easy_read: The aim of preparing financial statements is to know: - the performance of the enterprise - the financial position of the enterprise - the cash flows of the enterprise
pg015_n0020_easy_read: This includes finding out if the enterprise is making a profit or a loss. This is usually done by preparing an income statement. It also shows the financial wealth of the enterprise.
pg015_n0021_easy_read: This is done through the statement of financial position.
pg015_n0025_easy_read: Financial statements need to be analysed and explained to assess the performance of the enterprise.
pg015_n0026_easy_read: This is done by comparing the enterprise with other enterprises and by looking at the progress made from one period to another.
pg015_n0027_easy_read: One tool used to analyse financial statements is ratio analysis.
pg015_n0028_easy_read: Analysed financial information is useful to several users, such as: - owners - lenders - creditors This helps them make informed decisions.
pg015_n0032_easy_read: Modern book-keeping uses the double entry system.
pg015_n0033_easy_read: However, some businesses still find the single entry system adequate.
pg015_n0034_easy_read: The following are the two systems of book-keeping:
pg015_n0038_easy_read: Double-entry book-keeping is a more complete and widely used method. It gives a more accurate and detailed record of a business's financial transactions.
pg015_n0039_easy_read: It follows the rule that every transaction has equal and opposite effects on at least two accounts.
pg015_n0040_easy_read: Each transaction is recorded with: - a debit entry in one account - an equal credit entry in another account
pg015_n0041_easy_read: This method keeps a system of accounts, including: - assets - liabilities - equity - revenue - expenses
pg015_n0042_easy_read: Double-entry book-keeping keeps the accounting equation, open bracket, Assets equals Liabilities plus Equity, close bracket, balanced. It also allows the preparation of accurate financial statements, such as the statement of financial position and income statements.
pg016_n0003_easy_read: Roman numeral two. Single-entry Book-keeping: Single-entry book-keeping is a simple method. Small businesses or individuals mainly use it when they have few, repeated, and simple financial transactions.
pg016_n0004_easy_read: In this method, you make only one entry for each transaction. You usually record it in a revenue journal, an expense journal, or a cash book.
pg016_n0005_easy_read: Single-entry book-keeping records income and expenses. It does not track separate accounts for assets and liabilities.
pg016_n0006_easy_read: Single-entry book-keeping is used for basic record-keeping. For example, it tracks cash received and cash paid.
pg016_n0007_easy_read: The two book-keeping methods are different in how complex they are and in how much financial detail they give.
pg016_n0008_easy_read: Single-entry book-keeping is suitable for small businesses with simple transactions. Double-entry book-keeping is the standard method for most businesses because it is accurate, reliable, and gives a full financial overview.

pg016_n0019_easy_read: Assets are things that give benefits to the business.
pg016_n0020_easy_read: These assets include: - cash - inventory - equipment - property
pg016_n0022_easy_read: Roman numeral two. Liabilities: Liabilities are debts or duties a business owes to people or groups outside the business. Examples are: - loans - trade and other payables - accrued expenses
pg016_n0023_easy_read: The business has a duty to settle these obligations by using economic resources, for example cash.
pg016_n0026_easy_read: Expenses are costs a business has when it is generating revenue. These include: - salaries - rent - utilities - supplies - other operating expenses
pg016_n0029_easy_read: Debit entry: A debit entry is an entry on the left side of an account. It means: - an increase in assets - an increase in expenses - a decrease in liabilities - a decrease in revenue
pg016_n0031_easy_read: Roman numeral five. Credit entry: A credit entry is an entry on the right side of an account. It means: - an increase in liabilities - an increase in revenue - a decrease in assets - a decrease in expenses
pg016_n0036_easy_read: Account: An account is where financial transactions are recorded.
pg016_n0037_easy_read: An account is a basic part of book-keeping. It is used to track, organise, and summarise financial information.

pg017_n0006_easy_read: A debtor is a customer who buys goods or services from a business on credit.

pg017_n0008_easy_read: The person has an obligation to the business.
pg017_n0009_easy_read: The money that debtors owe to the business is an asset. The business treats it as a current asset in the statement of financial position.
pg017_n0010_easy_read: Another name for debtor is accounts receivable.
pg017_n0015_easy_read: A creditor is a person who sells goods or provides services on credit to a business.
pg017_n0016_easy_read: So, a creditor is a person that the business owes money to.
pg017_n0017_easy_read: The money that the business owes to creditors is a liability. The business treats it as a current liability in the statement of financial position.
pg017_n0018_easy_read: Another name for creditor is accounts payable.
pg017_n0023_easy_read: Trade receivables are money that customers owe to a business for goods or services sold on credit.
pg017_n0028_easy_read: Other receivables are amounts that people owe to the business, but not from sales of goods or services on credit to customers.
pg017_n0029_easy_read: An example of other receivables is money owed because the business lent money to its employees.
pg017_n0034_easy_read: Trade payables are money that a business owes to its creditors or suppliers for goods or services bought on credit.
pg017_n0039_easy_read: Other payables are amounts that the business owes from transactions other than buying goods for resale.
pg017_n0040_easy_read: An example is when the business buys a non-current asset on credit.
pg017_n0045_easy_read: A general ledger is the main record of all financial transactions of a business.

pg017_n0052_easy_read: It checks if debits are equal to credits. It also helps to find errors before preparing financial statements.
pg017_n0057_easy_read: Revenue is income that a business makes from its main activities, such as selling goods or services.
pg017_n0062_easy_read: Depreciation means spreading the cost of a long-term asset over its useful life. This matches the cost with the revenue the asset generates over its life.

pg017_n0068_easy_read: Cashflows can be cash coming in or cash going out.
pg018_n0004_easy_read: A business is any legal activity done to achieve a particular goal, such as making profit and reaching a planned level of service.
pg018_n0005_easy_read: Examples of business include: farming, a restaurant, a salon, and a kiosk.
pg018_n0008_easy_read: It is the money, or something worth money, that the owner provides to start or expand a business.

pg018_n0012_easy_read: A sole proprietor is the owner of a business who provides capital alone to start or expand the business.
pg018_n0013_easy_read: A sole proprietorship is a business that one person owns.
pg018_n0014_easy_read: In most cases, a sole proprietorship is a family business. It is the easiest type of business to start and run because the government does not regulate it a lot.
pg018_n0017_easy_read: Goods are items that the proprietor buys and sells. People can see and touch goods.
pg018_n0018_easy_read: Business people sell goods to meet the needs of customers.
pg018_n0019_easy_read: Examples of goods include: pens and exercise books for a stationeries business, food for a restaurant business, and cement for a hardware business.
pg018_n0022_easy_read: Services are activities that a business does. A business that gives services does not sell physical goods.
pg018_n0023_easy_read: Examples of services offered by different businesses are: hairdressing, drama shows, advertising, and training.
pg018_n0024_easy_read: Some businesses deal in both goods and services.
pg018_n0027_easy_read: Profit is the result a business gets when revenue is more than expenses for a particular period or activity.
pg018_n0028_easy_read: In other words, profit is the amount by which revenue is more than expenses for a particular period or activity.
pg018_n0031_easy_read: A business makes a loss when expenses are more than revenue for a particular period or activity.

pg025_n0011_easy_read: Under the revenue recognition principle, revenue should be recognised when it is realised or realisable and earned.
pg025_n0012_easy_read: This happens when these conditions are met:
pg025_n0016_easy_read: Identification of the contract: There should be a legal agreement between the seller and the buyer. The agreement should show the rights and duties of both parties.
pg025_n0019_easy_read: Delivery of goods or services: The seller has passed control of the goods or services to the buyer.
pg025_n0022_easy_read: Determination of the transaction price: The transaction price is fixed and can be estimated in a reasonable way.
pg025_n0023_easy_read: It includes the payment received or expected from the buyer for the goods or services.
pg025_n0026_easy_read: Collectability probability: It is likely that the seller will collect the amount the buyer should pay.
pg025_n0028_easy_read: Once these conditions are met, revenue should be recognised in the accounting records.
pg025_n0029_easy_read: The amount recognised is usually the fair value of the payment received or to be received for the goods or services provided.
pg025_n0030_easy_read: Revenue can be recognised at one point in time, for example when goods are delivered. Revenue can also be recognised over time, for example as services are provided.
pg025_n0031_easy_read: It is important to note that some industries or transactions may have extra guidance or standards for revenue recognition. Examples are long-term construction contracts and software sales.
pg025_n0032_easy_read: These rules for specific industries may give more conditions or guidance to show when revenue should be recognised.
pg025_n0034_easy_read: In summary, the revenue recognition principle says revenue should be recognised in the books when the sale of goods or services has been reasonably carried out, the amount is known, and the money has been collected or is reasonably expected to be collected.

pg026_n0023_easy_read: The materiality principle says financial information must be reported and shown if it can affect the decisions of people who use the financial statements.

pg026_n0026_easy_read: The materiality principle recognises that not all financial information is equally important.

pg026_n0029_easy_read: This principle encourages a person to use professional judgment to identify material information that needs clear and open disclosure in the financial statements.
pg026_n0030_easy_read: Information is material if adding it or leaving it out of the financial statements can affect the decisions of the users of the financial statements.
pg026_n0032_easy_read: The materiality principle accepts that financial statements should show a true and fair view of a business's financial position and performance.

Historical cost accounting is an accounting principle.
It says that an enterprise should record and report assets at their original cost when the enterprise acquires them.
pg027_n0010_easy_read: According to the historical cost principle, the first cost of an asset shows its value, even if its market value changes over time.
pg027_n0011_easy_read: Under the historical cost principle, when an enterprise acquires an asset, the enterprise records it in the statement of financial position (balance sheet) at the price paid to acquire or produce it.
pg027_n0012_easy_read:
This cost includes:
- the purchase price
- any extra costs to bring the asset to its present condition
- any extra costs to bring the asset to its present location
- transportation costs
- installation fees
pg027_n0014_easy_read: The purpose of the historical cost principle is to give a reliable and objective basis for financial reporting.
pg027_n0015_easy_read: When financial statements use the original cost of an asset, they show the actual resources the enterprise used at the time it acquired the asset.
pg027_n0016_easy_read: This principle supports consistency and makes financial statements easier to compare.
pg027_n0017_easy_read:
The historical cost principle avoids general estimates of an asset's value.
It also prevents changes to reported figures because of market changes.
pg027_n0019_easy_read: However, critics say that the historical cost principle may not show an asset's true value in a relevant and accurate way, especially for long-term assets like property, plant, and equipment.
pg027_n0020_easy_read:
Over time, the market value of assets may change because of:
- inflation
- technological advances
- changes in market conditions
pg027_n0021_easy_read: Some other valuation methods, such as fair value accounting, try to deal with these limits by valuing assets at their current market value.
pg027_n0022_easy_read: Even with its limits, the historical cost principle is still widely used in financial reporting, especially for assets that do not have clear market values.
pg027_n0023_easy_read:
It gives a conservative way to value assets.
It is also a basic principle in traditional accounting practices.
pg027_n0024_easy_read: The historical cost principle is in line with the going concern principle.
pg027_n0028_easy_read: This principle says that once an entity has chosen and used an accounting method or principle, the entity should keep using it for similar transactions and events in later periods.
pg027_n0029_easy_read:
In other words, an entity should not change its accounting methods or principles from one period to another without a good reason.
This can cause confusion and make it hard to compare financial information across different periods.
pg028_n0003_easy_read:
Consistency in accounting helps people compare financial statements better.
It helps users make clear comparisons and assess an entity’s financial performance and position over time.
pg028_n0004_easy_read:
If a change in accounting methods or principles is necessary, the change should include proper disclosure and justification.
This information is usually in the notes to the financial statements.
pg028_n0005_easy_read:
It is important to understand this:
The consistency principle does not mean accounting methods can never change or be updated.
pg028_n0006_easy_read: Changes in accounting standards, regulations, or circumstances may require changes to accounting methods.
pg028_n0007_easy_read:
However, people should make any changes carefully.
The aim should be to improve the relevance and reliability of financial information.
pg028_n0011_easy_read: Prudence, also called the conservatism principle, is an important concept in Book-keeping and accounting.
pg028_n0012_easy_read:
This principle means that when accountants face uncertainty or doubt, they should be careful.
They should choose the more conservative or prudent option.
pg028_n0013_easy_read:
In other words, it is better to make mistakes in this way:
- understate assets and revenues
- overstate liabilities and expenses
Rather than in this way:
- overstate assets and revenues
- understate liabilities and expenses
pg028_n0019_easy_read:
It is important to note this:
People should apply the prudence principle with care.
They should not use it to intentionally understate assets or income, or to overstate liabilities or expenses.
pg028_n0020_easy_read:
This principle aims to balance two things:
- caution
- giving a true and fair view of an entity’s financial position and performance

Every financial transaction affects two accounts in the enterprise.

Small businesses or individuals use it to track their financial transactions, mainly cash transactions.

These books are the first place where a business records all its transactions.
After that, the business posts them to the ledger or processes them further towards

This gives information about the transaction.

pg053_n0006_easy_read: So, it is good practice to record transactions in the books of prime entry in the order they happen.

pg053_n0053_easy_read:

The cash book records:

- money taken from the bank, bank withdrawals

A cash book is a book of prime entry.
It records transactions where cash moves in or out of the business.
This means the business receives cash or pays cash.

When the business receives cash, it records a debit entry in the cash book.
This increases assets.
When the business pays cash, it records a credit entry in the cash book.
This decreases the asset.

The cash book has a special feature.
It is a book of prime entry.
It is also part of the general ledger.

In an electronic system, the cash book is a digital record in accounting software or in an electronic spreadsheet.

- three column cash book
- petty cash book

pg054_n0030_easy_read:
Cash payments, such as expenses or loan repayments, are recorded on the credit side.
This is the right-hand side of the book.

pg067_n0030_easy_read: Sometimes a customer returns goods to the seller.
pg067_n0031_easy_read:
A customer may return goods for these reasons:
late delivery
low-quality goods
wrong type or specification, such as colour or size
damaged goods
expired goods
too many goods supplied
pg067_n0033_easy_read:
When a customer returns goods to a supplier, the supplier prepares and issues a credit note.
The credit note shows that the supplier has received the returned goods.
pg067_n0034_easy_read:
The purpose of the credit note is to tell the customer that the amount in the customer's account has been reduced.
This reduces the amount charged to the customer's account at the time of sale.
pg067_n0035_easy_read:
In this case, a credit note is a source document.
It is used to prepare the sales returns daybook.
pg067_n0036_easy_read: The sales returns journal has these columns:
pg068_n0005_easy_read: Use this column to write the date, month, and year of the transaction.
pg068_n0006_easy_read: This column shows when the transaction took place.
pg068_n0010_easy_read: This column gives a short description of the recorded transaction.
pg068_n0011_easy_read:
It records:
the name of the customer
the item
the reason for returning the goods
pg068_n0015_easy_read: This column records reference pages in the books of accounts.
pg068_n0016_easy_read: It shows the ledger and the page where the transaction was recorded.
pg068_n0020_easy_read: This column records the credit note number details. This number identifies the credit note issued when the return took place.
pg068_n0021_easy_read: This helps to check or investigate errors in the records. It makes it possible to find the credit notes, which are usually filed, and match them with the figures recorded in the books.
pg068_n0025_easy_read: This column records the details of the credit note for the return. It is useful when one credit note includes more than one type of goods returned.
pg068_n0029_easy_read: This column records the amount of money in the transaction. This is the price of the goods returned.

pg070_n0036_easy_read: When a business buys goods from a supplier, the business may sometimes need to return the goods to the seller.
pg070_n0037_easy_read: This may happen for reasons like the reasons given earlier for sales returns.
pg070_n0038_easy_read: When the buyer returns goods to the supplier, the supplier prepares a credit note. The credit note tells the buyer that the supplier has credited the buyer’s account.
pg070_n0039_easy_read: The credit note shows that the amount owed on the buyer’s account has gone down. This is because the correction has been made for the extra amount charged on the invoice.
pg070_n0040_easy_read: The credit note must clearly state the full reasons for returning the goods.
pg070_n0042_easy_read: Sometimes, the business may return the goods to the supplier with a debit note. This shows that the supplier’s account has been debited.
pg071_n0003_easy_read: People do not often use a debit note for this purpose these days.
pg071_n0004_easy_read: The return is fully confirmed when the seller accepts the returned goods and gives a credit note.
pg071_n0005_easy_read: So, the best practice is to use a credit note as proof of returned goods and as the source document for recording the return in the journal.

pg073_n0020_easy_read: The general journal is the first book used to record business transactions that are not recorded in special journals.
pg073_n0021_easy_read: Another name for the general journal is the journal proper. You can use both names to mean the same thing.
pg073_n0022_easy_read: Examples of entries recorded in the general journal are:
pg073_n0025_easy_read: item a. Buying or disposing of business assets that are not meant for sale.
pg073_n0029_easy_read: item c. Adjusting balances before preparing financial statements.
pg073_n0033_easy_read: item e. Opening entries used to find the capital of an ongoing business that did not use double entry before.
pg073_n0035_easy_read: The focus will be on examples of buying assets and opening entries.
pg073_n0036_easy_read: The other items will be covered later in higher forms.
pg073_n0037_easy_read: The general journal shows the double entries needed for different transactions. These are debit entries and credit entries. They follow the rules of debit and credit.
pg073_n0038_easy_read: As stated earlier, the general journal can be used to record all types of transactions made by the business.
pg073_n0039_easy_read: This is because the general journal shows clearly: the accounts; the side where each entry should be posted.
pg073_n0041_easy_read: However, if a business owner decides to use only a general journal and has credit dealings such as: sales; purchases; returns; then the business owner will need memorandum records, that is, schedules, with the details of those dealings.
pg074_n0003_easy_read: For this reason, entries in the general journal should focus on the general ledger.
pg074_n0004_easy_read: In other words, a general journal entry is not usually made for the individual account of a debtor or a creditor.
pg074_n0008_easy_read: A general journal has these functions:
pg074_n0012_easy_read: It works like a diary. It records business transactions as soon as they happen.
pg074_n0015_easy_read: It shows which accounts to debit and which accounts to credit for each transaction, following the rules of double entry.
pg074_n0018_easy_read: It gives a short description of each transaction recorded.
pg074_n0019_easy_read: This is very important because, unlike the special journals, the general journal records different types of transactions.
pg074_n0022_easy_read: The transactions are recorded in date order and include short descriptions. This makes it easier for a person to review the records and find possible recording errors.
pg074_n0040_easy_read: The name of the account to debit.
pg074_n0041_easy_read: The name of the account to credit.

pg116_n0005_easy_read: A ledger is a basic part of the double entry accounting system.
pg116_n0006_easy_read: A ledger is used to keep a detailed and organised record of all financial transactions in a business.
pg116_n0007_easy_read: A ledger is the main place where individual accounts are kept. It shows how each transaction affects: assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses.
pg116_n0008_easy_read: The ledger helps to keep records accurate and complete. It records both debit and credit entries for every transaction. This makes it easy to track and analyse the business's financial position and performance.
pg116_n0009_easy_read: Ledgers can be kept by hand in physical books or electronically using computer software. They give a full and up-to-date view of the business's financial activities.
pg116_n0011_easy_read: In the ledger, each account is shown in a T-shape format. Debits are on the left side. Credits are on the right side.
pg116_n0012_easy_read: The ledger is a detailed reference for organising financial data into specific accounts.
pg116_n0013_easy_read: The ledger makes it easier for accountants and financial analysts to prepare financial statements and carry out audits.
pg116_n0014_easy_read: Through the ledger, businesses can: monitor the flow of funds, track revenue and expenses, identify patterns or irregularities, and ensure compliance with accounting standards.
pg116_n0015_easy_read: The ledger must be accurate and reliable. This helps stakeholders understand the business's financial health clearly. It also helps them make informed decisions to support the business's success.

The trial balance is very important in accounting.
It checks accuracy, finds errors, and helps to prepare financial statements.
pg120_n0010_easy_read:
The trial balance helps to keep financial data accurate.
This leads to reliable financial reports and better decisions in a business or enterprise.

Extracting a trial balance is a basic part of accounting.
It is also an important step in the accounting cycle.
pg120_n0024_easy_read: A trial balance is a list of balances taken from general ledger accounts on a particular date.
pg120_n0025_easy_read: In simple words, a trial balance is a picture of the balances in ledger accounts on a specific date.
pg120_n0026_easy_read: You prepare a trial balance by using debit and credit balances taken from general ledger accounts.
pg120_n0027_easy_read: In chapter five, you learnt that entries are posted to general ledger accounts by following the double entry principle of book-keeping.
pg120_n0028_easy_read: This means the trial balance should always balance.
pg120_n0029_easy_read: In other words, if you post the entry in the ledger accounts correctly, the total debit balances and the total credit balances must be equal.
pg120_n0033_easy_read: A trial balance has the following advantages for an enterprise:
pg121_n0005_easy_read: A trial balance lists debit and credit balances taken from the general ledgers.
pg121_n0006_easy_read: Then, these balances are used to prepare financial statements.
pg121_n0007_easy_read: In simple terms, balances move from the ledgers to the trial balance, and then from the trial balance to the financial statements.
pg121_n0008_easy_read: A person does not need to go back to each general ledger account to find balances when preparing financial statements.
pg121_n0011_easy_read: Financial statements are financial reports made at the end of the accounting period.
pg121_n0012_easy_read: Examples of financial statements are: an income statement; a statement of financial position.
pg121_n0016_easy_read: The trial balance is prepared from debit and credit balances taken from general ledger accounts.
pg121_n0017_easy_read: The trial balance should balance at any time because entries in the general ledger accounts follow the double entry principle.
pg121_n0018_easy_read: So, if the trial balance does not balance, it may mean there are errors in the posting process.
pg121_n0019_easy_read: Because of this, the trial balance is used to find errors made during the posting process.
pg121_n0023_easy_read: If entries in ledger accounts are done wrongly, the trial balance will not balance.
pg121_n0024_easy_read: In this way, the trial balance is used to check if the double entries made to the accounts are correct.
pg121_n0028_easy_read: Double entries may be done correctly, but mistakes can still happen when people calculate the posted figures.
pg121_n0029_easy_read: Mistakes in the calculation will cause incorrect balances to be taken from the ledger accounts.
pg121_n0030_easy_read: This will stop the trial balance from balancing.
pg121_n0031_easy_read: So, the trial balance checks whether the figures on the trial balance were calculated correctly.
pg121_n0035_easy_read: The trial balance is a summary of debit and credit balances taken from the general ledger.
pg121_n0036_easy_read: In the trial balance, balances from the general ledger accounts are listed in a clear order.
pg121_n0040_easy_read: A trial balance is important to the entity, but it also has limitations.
pg121_n0041_easy_read: The main limitation of the trial balance is that it cannot find all possible errors in the ledger accounts.
pg121_n0042_easy_read: This means that equal total debit and credit balances are not enough to show that there was no error when posting transactions to the general ledger accounts.
pg121_n0043_easy_read: This is because some errors may still be there even when the total credit and debit balances agree.
pg121_n0044_easy_read: For example, a wrong amount is posted for a
pg122_n0003_easy_read: A transaction may have both the debit and credit entries posted with the wrong amount, or one posting may go to the wrong account.
pg122_n0004_easy_read: In these cases, the trial balance can still agree even when there are errors in posting.
pg122_n0006_easy_read: Also, the trial balance does not:
pg122_n0010_easy_read: Show that all transactions have been recorded.
pg122_n0013_easy_read: Find a missing entry in the journals or in the ledger.
pg122_n0019_easy_read: Show that the ledger is correct, and
pg122_n0024_easy_read: In short, a trial balance does not guarantee that recording entries will be free from errors.

Extracting a trial balance is a key step in the accounting process or cycle.
It summarises the balances of all ledger accounts at a specific time.
pg133_n0116_easy_read:
A trial balance is very important in the double-entry accounting system.
It gives a first check to make sure the financial records are accurate.
pg133_n0117_easy_read:
The trial balance lists all general ledger accounts.
It also shows their debit balances and credit balances.
pg133_n0118_easy_read:
Businesses compare the total debits and total credits.
This helps them check that the accounting equation is in balance:
Assets equals Liabilities plus Equity.
pg133_n0119_easy_read:
If the trial balance balances, it suggests that the double-entry accounting system was used correctly.
It also shows that total debits equal total credits.
pg133_n0120_easy_read:
However, a balanced trial balance does not guarantee that there are no errors.
Some mistakes may cancel each other.
This can make the records look correct even when they are not.
pg134_n0003_easy_read:
A balanced trial balance shows overall accuracy.
But it does not show the exact errors.
pg134_n0004_easy_read:
A trial balance is a useful tool for finding some mistakes, such as:
- transposition errors
- omissions
But it may not show more difficult errors, such as:
- incorrect postings
- compensating errors
pg134_n0005_easy_read:
So, accountants should do more analysis and reconciliation.
This helps to make sure the financial records are correct.
pg134_n0006_easy_read:
The trial balance is an important step in accounting.
People usually prepare it at the end of an accounting period.
It helps to prepare financial statements.
It also gives a starting point for more detailed financial analysis and decision-making.

They help people make informed decisions.
They also help people assess:
- profitability
- solvency
- liquidity
- the overall financial health of the business
