pg139_n0019_easy_read:
This section explains:
- the meaning of financial statements
- the purposes of financial statements
- the common users of financial statements
pg139_n0025_easy_read:
Financial statements are prepared at regular times.
They show the results of the business for that period.
pg139_n0027_easy_read:
Financial statements have five components.
This text focuses on two components:
- the income statement
- the statement of financial position
pg139_n0028_easy_read:
The income statement is also called a statement of profit or loss.
A business prepares it to find out if it made a profit or a loss in a particular accounting period.
pg139_n0029_easy_read:
The statement of financial position is also called a balance sheet.
A business prepares it to show its financial position.
It does this by looking at the balances of:
- assets
- liabilities
- capital
pg139_n0031_easy_read:
Some businesses must prepare financial statements by law.
For example, companies must do this.
pg140_n0003_easy_read:
Financial statements may not be required by law, except for tax purposes.
But financial statements can still meet the needs of the owners, especially when they want to check the business performance for the period.
pg140_n0004_easy_read: Other people can also benefit from the financial statements of a business.
pg140_n0005_easy_read: This is because understanding the financial and operating affairs of the business can help them make informed decisions.
pg140_n0009_easy_read: The detailed purposes of preparing financial statements are:
pg140_n0013_easy_read: Many businesses are set up to make profits.
pg140_n0014_easy_read: So, it is important to measure if the business has achieved this objective.
pg140_n0015_easy_read: This is because owners can check if the management has met their targets.
pg140_n0016_easy_read: It also helps owners decide whether to continue with the business.
pg140_n0020_easy_read: When a business gets into a difficult financial position, for example when it has too many liabilities, it may face the risk of closing because it cannot pay its debts.
pg140_n0021_easy_read: In the same way, when a business has a large share of its assets in non-productive assets, the business may fail in the future.
pg140_n0022_easy_read: On the other hand, a good share of productive assets shows a bright future for the business.
pg140_n0026_easy_read: Non-productive assets are assets in the business that are not fully used to generate revenue.
pg140_n0027_easy_read: For example, a large office building that is more than the business needs may be a non-productive asset.
pg140_n0031_easy_read: Efficient business operations help the business achieve its profit-making objective.
pg140_n0032_easy_read: Examples of efficiency measures include: assets utilisation; and frequency of stock movements, or stock turnover.
pg140_n0033_easy_read: Assets utilisation measures how well the business is using its available assets to make money.
pg140_n0034_easy_read: Stock turnover measures how many times a business has sold and replaced its inventory during a given period.
pg140_n0035_easy_read: The figures used to calculate ratios for these measures usually come from financial statements.
pg140_n0036_easy_read: When the level of efficiency is unsatisfactory, the business can plan ways to improve its performance.
pg140_n0040_easy_read: The business works out the amounts of different taxes it must pay from the figures in the financial statements.
pg140_n0041_easy_read: Profit and sales figures give a reasonable basis for calculating taxes related to turnover or profits.
pg140_n0042_easy_read: These figures can be easily taken from the business financial statements.
pg141_n0005_easy_read: Planning and evaluation are two main functions of management.
pg141_n0006_easy_read: Financial statements help to evaluate how a business performed during the period.
pg141_n0007_easy_read: People can do this by comparing the targets set at the beginning of the year with the actual results in the financial statements.
pg141_n0008_easy_read: Also, the performance of the current year can be the basis for plans for the next year.
pg141_n0012_easy_read: Different stakeholders who deal with the business, for example: banks, customers, and suppliers, need to be sure about the risk linked to the business.
pg141_n0013_easy_read: In this context, risk means the chance that actual results will be different from expected results.
pg141_n0014_easy_read: Traditionally, risk means the possibility of: danger, loss, injury, and other negative outcomes.
pg141_n0015_easy_read: For example, customers want to be sure they will keep getting goods regularly. Banks and suppliers want to be sure the business can pay its debts.
pg141_n0016_easy_read: Financial statements show the results of business performance. So, people usually see them as a reliable source of information.
pg141_n0017_easy_read: This information helps stakeholders to answer their questions, including questions about the risks linked to the business.
pg141_n0021_easy_read: Various stakeholders use financial statements, including: investors, creditors, management, and regulators. They use them to check the financial health of the business and make informed decisions.
pg141_n0022_easy_read: The three common components of financial statements are:
pg141_n0026_easy_read: The income statement shows the financial performance of a business from its operating activities over a specific period, for example, a quarter or a year.
pg141_n0027_easy_read: It gives a summary of revenues, expenses, and the final profit or loss.
pg141_n0028_easy_read: The income statement uses this basic formula:
pg141_n0031_easy_read: Key figures in the income statement are:
pg141_n0038_easy_read: Cost of goods sold, C O G S, for businesses that sell products.
pg141_n0041_easy_read: Gross profit, revenues minus cost of goods sold.
pg141_n0044_easy_read: Operating expenses, selling, general, and administrative expenses.
pg141_n0047_easy_read: Operating income, gross profit minus operating expenses.
pg141_n0050_easy_read: Other income and expenses, interest income and interest expenses.
pg141_n0053_easy_read: Profit or loss for the period.
pg141_n0057_easy_read: The statement of financial position shows the financial position of a business at a specific time, usually at the end of a quarter or a year.
pg141_n0058_easy_read: It shows the resources of the business, assets, and what the business owes to
pg142_n0003_easy_read: other debts of the business, liabilities, and the owners' remaining interest, equity.
pg142_n0005_easy_read: The statement of financial position follows this accounting equation:
pg142_n0007_easy_read: The main parts of a statement of financial position are:
pg142_n0017_easy_read: Capital or equity: money invested in a business; initial capital; retained earnings.
pg142_n0021_easy_read: The cash flow statement gives an overview of the cash coming into and going out of an enterprise over a specific period.
pg142_n0022_easy_read: The cash flow statement shows how the enterprise gets cash and uses cash during the period through: operating activities; investing activities; financing activities.
pg142_n0023_easy_read: The cash flow statement has three sections:
pg142_n0027_easy_read: Operating activities: Cash flows from the day-to-day work of the business. This includes cash received from customers and cash paid to suppliers and employees.
pg142_n0030_easy_read: Investing activities: Cash flows from buying or selling long-term assets, such as property, equipment, or investments.
pg142_n0033_easy_read: Financing activities: Cash flows from transactions with the enterprise's owners and loan providers. This includes: issuing or buying back shares; getting or repaying a loan; paying dividends.
pg142_n0035_easy_read: These parts of financial statements are important for checking an enterprise’s: financial performance; liquidity; solvency; overall financial health.
pg142_n0036_easy_read: Together, these financial statements give a full view of the enterprise’s financial position. They also help in decision-making and financial analysis.
pg142_n0037_easy_read: This chapter will discuss only the income statement and the statement of financial position. Cash flow statements will be discussed in higher forms.
pg142_n0041_easy_read: An income statement is prepared at the end of an accounting period to calculate the profit or loss made.
pg142_n0042_easy_read: The income statement calculates profit or loss for the period by comparing revenue earned during the period with expenses incurred during the same period.
pg142_n0043_easy_read: The matching principle is applied in the income statement, as shown in chapter one.
pg142_n0047_easy_read: The purpose of preparing an income statement is to calculate the amount of profit or loss for a particular period.
pg142_n0048_easy_read: A merchandising business calculates profit or loss in two stages.
pg142_n0049_easy_read: The first stage compares net sales with the cost of goods sold to get the gross profit or gross loss.
pg142_n0050_easy_read: The second stage compares the gross profit from the first stage and other incomes with the different expenses of operating the business during the period.
pg142_n0051_easy_read: The result is the profit or loss for the period.
pg143_n0005_easy_read: These are the terms used in an income statement:
pg143_n0009_easy_read: Net sales has two parts: sales; sales returns.
pg143_n0010_easy_read: The sales figure is the credit balance moved from the sales account in the general ledger.
pg143_n0011_easy_read: The sales figure is the total of all sales, both credit and cash, made during the period.
pg143_n0012_easy_read: Sales returns are goods that were sold to a customer before, but the customer later returned them for different reasons.
pg143_n0013_easy_read: So, net sales is sales minus sales returns. Sales returns are also called returns inwards.
pg143_n0017_easy_read: The net purchases figure comes after you consider several parts.
pg143_n0018_easy_read: The first part is the debit balance in the purchases account itself.
pg143_n0019_easy_read: This figure is the total purchases, both cash and credit, made during the whole accounting period.
pg143_n0021_easy_read: The second part used to calculate net purchases is purchases returns, also called returns outwards.
pg143_n0022_easy_read: Purchases returns are goods that the entity bought before, but later returned to the supplier for different reasons.
pg143_n0023_easy_read: The purchases figure shows the total amount of purchases, both credit and cash. It does not deduct goods returned to the supplier.
pg143_n0024_easy_read: So, to get net purchases, deduct purchases returns from purchases.
pg143_n0026_easy_read: The full equation is: net purchases equals purchases minus purchases returns.
pg143_n0028_easy_read: The aim of this process is to calculate the cost of goods sold. Another cost included in this is carriage inwards costs.
pg143_n0029_easy_read: These are the costs of moving or transporting purchased goods from where the enterprise bought them to the enterprise's premises.
pg143_n0030_easy_read: In simple words, the cost of goods purchased is: the amount paid to buy the goods; plus the transport cost to bring the goods to the enterprise's premises.
pg143_n0031_easy_read: For example, a supplier sold goods for T Z S one hundred thousand. The buyer also paid T Z S ten thousand to transport the goods from the supplier's premises to the buyer's premises.
pg143_n0032_easy_read: In this case, the cost of the goods is not only Tanzanian shillings one hundred thousand. It is Tanzanian shillings one hundred and ten thousand, that is, Tanzanian shillings one hundred thousand plus ten thousand.
pg143_n0036_easy_read: Opening inventory is the stock of goods the entity has at the beginning of the accounting period.
pg143_n0037_easy_read: Closing inventory is the stock of goods the entity has at the end of the accounting period.
pg143_n0038_easy_read: For example, the enterprise's accounting period starts on first January and ends on thirty-first December.
pg143_n0039_easy_read: The opening inventory of that enterprise is the inventory it has on first January. The closing inventory is the inventory it has on thirty-first December.

pg144_n0007_easy_read: The cost of goods available for sale is the opening inventory plus net purchases.
pg144_n0011_easy_read: The cost of goods sold is the cost of goods available for sale minus closing inventory.
pg144_n0012_easy_read: In other words, subtract the cost of closing inventory from the cost of goods available for sale to get the cost of goods sold.
pg144_n0016_easy_read: Gross profit is the net sales figure minus the cost of goods sold.
pg144_n0017_easy_read: Gross profit is the profit that an enterprise gets from trading activities only. It does not include other operating expenses.
pg144_n0021_easy_read: Gross loss is the cost of goods sold minus net sales.
pg144_n0022_easy_read: Gross loss means the cost of goods sold is more than net sales.
pg144_n0026_easy_read: You can calculate profit or loss by subtracting the total expenses for the period from the total revenue.
pg144_n0027_easy_read: Profit means total revenue is more than total expenses.
pg144_n0028_easy_read: Loss means total expenses are more than total revenue.
pg144_n0032_easy_read: Gross profit is the difference between net sales and the cost of goods sold.
pg144_n0033_easy_read: Net sales is the balance in the sales account in the general ledger at the end of a period.
pg144_n0034_easy_read: However, some goods sold during the period may be returned.
pg144_n0035_easy_read: In this case, use the net sales figure in the income statement. Net sales means sales minus sales returns.
pg144_n0036_easy_read: The sales returns figure comes from the sales returns account in the general ledger.
pg144_n0038_easy_read: For the cost of goods sold, the main part is the value of purchases.
pg144_n0039_easy_read: In some cases, use the net purchases figure instead.
pg144_n0040_easy_read: For the same reason as sales returns, if some goods were returned to suppliers, subtract them from the purchases figure.
pg144_n0041_easy_read: The purchases figure, or net purchases, can also be adjusted by adding the cost of transporting the goods to the business premises.
pg144_n0042_easy_read: This cost is also called carriage inwards.
pg144_n0043_easy_read: The figure for this cost is the balance in the carriage inwards account in the general ledger.

pg150_n0012_easy_read: An income statement shows financial performance for a period. This means profit or loss for that period. A statement of financial position is different. It shows the financial position of a business on a specific date.
pg150_n0013_easy_read: The specific date is the end of the accounting period.
pg150_n0014_easy_read: Businesses prepare a statement of financial position. It shows the financial position of the business on the date written on the statement.
pg150_n0016_easy_read: The statement of financial position shows the relationship between: assets, liabilities, capital.
pg150_n0017_easy_read: You may remember this basic accounting equation: assets equals liabilities plus capital
pg150_n0018_easy_read: The statement of financial position shows how this equation stands at the end of the accounting period. It looks at each of these elements: assets, liabilities, capital.
pg150_n0019_easy_read: It is called a statement of financial position because it shows: the assets of the business, and how those assets were financed. This financing is shown by the proportions of liabilities and capital.
pg150_n0023_easy_read: When preparing a statement of financial position, the value of each type of asset and liability usually comes from the general ledger balances.
pg150_n0024_easy_read: To help users understand the financial position of the business, assets and liabilities are presented in an orderly way. They are not listed randomly.

pg152_n0005_easy_read: People usually group assets and liabilities into current and non-current using the accounting period being looked at.
pg152_n0006_easy_read: In this classification, the following groups of assets and liabilities are included.
pg152_n0010_easy_read: Current assets include cash and other assets that a business mainly holds for trading.
pg152_n0011_easy_read: The business usually expects to realise current assets in its normal operating cycle and within the next accounting period.
pg152_n0012_easy_read: In other words, current assets are either cash, at bank or in hand, or assets that the business will convert into cash within the next accounting period during normal business operations.
pg152_n0013_easy_read: Examples of current assets are: inventory, accounts receivable, cash at bank, and cash in hand.
pg152_n0017_easy_read: Non-current assets are all assets that are not current assets. The business expects to use them to support business operations for more than one year or accounting period.
pg152_n0018_easy_read: Examples of non-current assets are: land, building, furniture, vehicles, plants, and machinery owned by the business.
pg152_n0022_easy_read: Current liabilities are liabilities that must be paid within one year or accounting period.
pg152_n0023_easy_read: For this reason, current liabilities are also called short term debts.
pg152_n0024_easy_read: Examples of current liabilities are: creditors, trade payables, and bank overdrafts.
pg152_n0028_easy_read: Non-current liabilities are all liabilities that are not current liabilities. They become due after one year.
pg152_n0029_easy_read: For this reason, non-current liabilities are also called long term debts.
pg152_n0030_easy_read: Examples of non-current liabilities are: bank loans and a term loan from a friend.

The information in financial statements is useful to different users.
It depends on what they need the information for.
pg158_n0016_easy_read: Here is a list of common users of financial statements and why they need this information.
pg158_n0020_easy_read: Managers want the information in financial statements to know how the business is performing.
pg158_n0021_easy_read: Financial statements can also help managers to make future plans.
pg158_n0024_easy_read: These are people who invested their money or other resources in the business to make a profit.
pg158_n0025_easy_read: So, they are interested in the information in the financial statements because it helps them to evaluate their business against the profit target.
pg158_n0028_easy_read: These are people who want to put in their money to invest in, or buy part or all of, a business so they can benefit from the profit it makes.
pg158_n0029_easy_read:
Before a prospective investor or buyer buys a business, the person will want to see its financial statements.
This helps the person evaluate the business's ability to make profits.
pg158_n0030_easy_read: This information is very important for making an informed decision about whether to invest in the business or not.
pg158_n0033_easy_read: A person, or entity, who puts money into a business to become one of the owners and get a share of the profit made.
pg158_n0036_easy_read:
Tax officers from tax authorities, such as the Tanzania Revenue Authority, T R A, and the Zanzibar Revenue Authority, Z R A, want to see the financial statements of an enterprise.
They do this to check if the calculations are correct and to find the amount of tax the enterprise must pay.
pg158_n0039_easy_read: Banks that the entrepreneur may go to for loans and other services will want to know the business performance trend so they can make
pg159_n0003_easy_read: decisions about whether to lend money or not.
pg159_n0004_easy_read:
For example, the bank may want to see the financial statements.
The bank uses them to check if the business can repay the loan it is asking for.
pg159_n0008_easy_read:
Creditors or payables are suppliers of goods or services.
They sell goods or provide services to the business on credit.
pg159_n0009_easy_read:
Creditors want the information in the financial statements.
They use it to check if debtors can pay for the goods and services they got on credit when payment is due.
pg159_n0013_easy_read: Debtors or receivables are businesses or people who buy goods or services from the business on credit.
pg159_n0014_easy_read:
Debtors do not usually use the financial statements of their creditors.
But sometimes they need them, especially cash flow statements.
They use them to check if the creditors can keep supplying goods regularly, especially in tender businesses.
pg159_n0018_easy_read:
Basic financial statements are key documents.
They give a full picture of a business's financial performance and financial position.
pg159_n0019_easy_read:
These statements are very important for stakeholders, such as:
- investors
- creditors
- managers

They help them check the financial health of the business and make informed decisions.
pg159_n0020_easy_read:
Financial statements include:
- statement of financial position, balance sheet
- income statement
- cash flow statement
pg159_n0022_easy_read:
The statement of financial position gives a summary of the enterprise's financial position at a specific time.
It shows its assets, liabilities, and equity.
pg159_n0023_easy_read:
The statement of financial position shows the accounting equation:
Assets equals liabilities plus equity.
It also shows how the business' resources are financed.
pg159_n0024_easy_read:
The income statement shows the business's:
- revenues
- expenses
- net income
- net loss

It covers a specific period, usually a quarter or a year.
pg159_n0025_easy_read:
It shows the business's profitability.
It does this by comparing revenue with expenses.
pg159_n0026_easy_read: The cash flow statement shows the business's cash coming in and cash going out during a given period.
pg159_n0027_easy_read:
It groups the cash flows into:
- operating activities
- investing activities
- financing activities
pg159_n0028_easy_read:
This statement shows the business's ability to generate cash and manage cash.
This is important for its sustainability and growth.
pg159_n0029_easy_read:
Together, these basic financial statements give a clear and full picture of a business's financial performance and financial position.
They help stakeholders measure:
- profitability
- solvency
- liquidity
